title: Septic shock, one machine, and the question of when
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module text; no drug doses are given. Your unit’s protocols, the intensive care team and the attending nephrologist decide every order.
intro:
You are the first-year nephrology fellow at a tertiary hospital in Iloilo City. Mrs. Lourdes Villareal, 66, a retired public school teacher who weighs about 60 kg, was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) yesterday with septic shock from a kidney infection. She is intubated and on norepinephrine at a low, steady rate.

Her creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 3.1 mg/dL, more than three times baseline: acute kidney injury (AKI) stage 3 by the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. She passes 20 to 30 mL of urine an hour. Potassium is 5.3 mmol/L, pH 7.30 with a bicarbonate of 17 mmol/L, oxygen needs are stable, and her fluid balance is plus 3.1 liters. The hospital’s only continuous kidney replacement therapy (CKRT) machine is in use by another patient this week. It has one standard hemodialysis machine on wheels, a portable water system, and a dialysis nurse on call. The ICU consultant asks whether you will start kidney replacement therapy (KRT) today “to get ahead of it.”

n1.prompt: What do you answer the ICU consultant?

choices.text: Start KRT today. In septic shock, an early start is the safer choice.
choices.feedback: Four randomized trials tested this. An accelerated start did not lower mortality in any of them, and in STARRT-AKI it was associated with more dialysis dependence among survivors (10.4% vs 6.0%) and more adverse events (23.0% vs 16.5%).
choices.then: Your attending advises waiting with a written list of start triggers, checked every shift. You write it.

choices.text: Not today: she has no urgent indication. Write the triggers you are watching (potassium, pH, oxygen and balance, uremic signs), recheck them every shift, and confirm tonight that the machine and a dialysis nurse can be reached.
choices.feedback: Start for the urgent indication, not the creatinine. In AKIKI, 49% of the delayed group never received KRT. AKIKI 2 showed the limit of waiting too long, so the plan names what will make you start.

choices.text: Wait, and recheck her laboratory tests on tomorrow’s rounds.
choices.feedback: Waiting is right. But a plan with no written triggers and no shift-by-shift checks lets watchful waiting drift into neglect.
choices.then: You add a written trigger list, rechecked every shift, before you leave the ICU.

choices.text: Run a standard four-hour hemodialysis tonight and take off the 3 liters she has gained.
choices.feedback: She has no urgent indication, and fast fluid removal in a patient on a vasopressor can drop her pressure and injure a kidney that may be starting to recover.
choices.then: The attending stops the order before it starts and asks for a written trigger list instead.

n2.scene: The intern calls you. Potassium is 6.5 mmol/L and the electrocardiogram (ECG) shows peaked T waves. pH is 7.18 with a bicarbonate of 12 mmol/L. She has passed 5 mL an hour for 10 hours, her oxygen needs are rising, and the chest film shows new haziness in both lungs. The norepinephrine rate is climbing.
n2.prompt: What happens in the next hour?

choices.text: The hyperkalemia protocol now as a bridge; call the attending; a temporary catheter under ultrasound guidance, right internal jugular first; consent from the family; review platelets, clotting and the medicines that will need dose review; confirm the machine, water and nurse.
choices.feedback: She now has three urgent indications: hyperkalemia with ECG changes, overload with rising oxygen needs, and severe acidemia on a rising vasopressor. The protocol buys time; KRT is what you use when that time runs out. KDIGO recommends ultrasound guidance for catheter insertion (1A) and lists the right internal jugular first among sites (not graded).

choices.text: The hyperkalemia protocol now; place the catheter on morning rounds, when the full team is in.
choices.feedback: The bridge is right, but it is a bridge. With three urgent indications, morning is hours of risk away.
choices.then: At 03:30 potassium is 6.4 mmol/L despite the protocol. The attending asks you to place the catheter now.

choices.text: Repeat the potassium first and wait for the result before calling anyone.
choices.feedback: A repeat is reasonable, but alongside the protocol and the call, not instead of them. ECG changes make this urgent whatever the repeat shows.
choices.then: The repeat is 6.6 mmol/L. You start the protocol, call the attending and place the catheter.

choices.text: Give a diuretic and recheck the potassium in six hours.
choices.feedback: In near-anuria a diuretic will not lower potassium quickly, and six hours is far too long with ECG changes. KDIGO advises diuretics in AKI only to manage volume overload (2C), never as a delay to KRT.
choices.then: The nurse calls you back at 03:15: the T waves are taller. You start the protocol, call the attending and place the catheter.

n3.scene: The catheter is in. The CKRT machine is still in use. You have the standard hemodialysis machine, the portable water system, and a dialysis nurse who can stay the whole session.

choices.text: Insert a peritoneal catheter and start acute peritoneal dialysis.
choices.feedback: The International Society for Peritoneal Dialysis (ISPD) 2020 guideline calls it suitable for AKI in all settings (1B), and it is gentle. But it is slower to clear potassium, she already has a working blood catheter and a machine, and tonight her potassium is the emergency.
choices.then: The attending prefers the blood circuit tonight for the potassium and keeps peritoneal dialysis as the backup.

choices.text: Standard four-hour hemodialysis, removing her excess fluid in the same session.
choices.feedback: It clears potassium fastest, but in shock on a rising vasopressor a short session with large fluid removal risks hypotension.
choices.then: Before starting, the attending asks you to run the session longer at lower flows, with slow fluid removal.

choices.text: Bridge with medicines until the CKRT machine is free tomorrow.
choices.feedback: She has three urgent indications now. Medical measures buy an hour or two, not a day.
choices.then: At 05:00 potassium is back to 6.7 mmol/L. The attending tells you to start on the standard machine at once.

choices.text: Sustained low-efficiency dialysis (SLED) on the standard machine: longer session, lower flows, potassium and acid first, fluid removal slow and titrated to her pressure with the ICU team.
choices.feedback: KDIGO suggests CKRT rather than standard intermittent KRT for unstable patients (2B); prolonged therapy was not what it compared against. In a trial of 232 surgical ICU patients, 90-day mortality was 49.6% with SLED and 55.6% with hemofiltration (not significant), and a meta-analysis of 7 randomized trials found no mortality difference.

n4.scene: Her platelets are 52,000 per microliter and the catheter site is oozing. The pharmacy has no citrate.

choices.text: Unfractionated heparin per the unit’s standard intermittent protocol.
choices.feedback: KDIGO’s heparin recommendation for intermittent KRT (1C) is for patients without increased bleeding risk. She has low platelets and an oozing site.
choices.then: The attending changes the order to no anticoagulation. The circuit clots once; the nurse changes it and the session continues.

choices.text: None. Keep the blood flow adequate, watch the catheter position, avoid hemoconcentration in the filter, plan shorter runs, and write the reason in the order.
choices.feedback: Without citrate, and with a high bleeding risk, running without anticoagulation is the usual trade. Expect more clotting, and do not add heparin by reflex if a filter clots in a bleeding patient.

choices.text: Switch to acute peritoneal dialysis, which needs no anticoagulation at all.
choices.feedback: That is one real reason to consider peritoneal dialysis in a bleeding patient. But tonight the blood circuit is primed and her potassium is still high; running it without anticoagulation is the faster safe route.
choices.then: You keep the blood circuit and run it without anticoagulation; peritoneal dialysis stays the backup.

choices.text: Run without anticoagulation, but give heparin whenever the filter clots, and more with each clot.
choices.feedback: Adding heparin by reflex in a patient with low platelets and active oozing trades a clotted filter for bleeding she may not survive. A clot means a new circuit, not systemic anticoagulation.
choices.then: After the second clot the nurse calls you. The attending stops the heparin; the catheter site keeps oozing for hours.

n5.scene: She was extubated yesterday and is off norepinephrine. Over the last 24 hours she passed 1,100 mL of urine without any diuretic. Potassium and pH have stayed controlled since her last session. The ICU consultant asks: “Can we stop?”

choices.text: Continue daily SLED until her creatinine is back to normal.
choices.feedback: The creatinine is not the trigger to stop. Every day on KRT carries catheter, hypotension and cost risk; the question is whether the original indications are gone and the urine is returning.
choices.then: The attending asks you to hold the next session and watch.

choices.text: Give a diuretic to increase the urine, then decide.
choices.feedback: KDIGO suggests not using diuretics to enhance recovery or to reduce the duration or frequency of KRT (2B). Urine produced by diuretics also predicts successful stopping less well than spontaneous urine.
choices.then: You leave the diuretic off, hold the next session and watch.

choices.text: Hold the next session; check potassium, acid-base, volume and urine every shift; restart if an urgent indication returns; plan to remove the catheter once KRT is no longer expected.
choices.feedback: KRT should stop when it is no longer required (KDIGO, not graded). In an observational study of patients coming off CKRT, urine output in the 24 hours before stopping was the strongest predictor of success, and less so when diuretics were given. Every catheter day is infection risk.

choices.text: Stop KRT and remove the catheter today; no more potassium checks are needed now that the urine is back.
choices.feedback: Stopping may be right, but the watching is not optional. Potassium, acid and fluid can rebound in the days after the last session, and you need to know before it becomes an emergency.
choices.then: The attending restores the shift-by-shift checks for the next three days.

end.title: Day 12
end.text: She needed no further sessions. The catheter came out on day 10, and on day 12 she moved to the ward with a creatinine still above baseline: acute kidney disease, not a healed kidney. Her discharge plan follows Module 9: the peak and discharge creatinine, the medicines held, a test within two weeks and a review at three months.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Start KRT for the urgent indication, not the creatinine. Everyone else gets a written trigger list, rechecked every shift.
  • When the urgent indications arrive, bridge and prepare together: the protocol, the call, an ultrasound-guided catheter, consent and the machine.
  • Choose what her circulation tolerates and the hospital can run all night: SLED on a standard machine, or acute peritoneal dialysis, is real care when done well.
  • Match anticoagulation to bleeding risk and stock, and write the reason. A clot in a bleeding patient means a new circuit, not more heparin.
  • Ask “can we stop?” every day, and let spontaneous urine answer.

See When to start, Which modality, Anticoagulation and Liberation.
